title.rendered: Chest Pain: Muscular, Lung, or Heart? Key Differences

content.rendered:
Chest pain is one of the scariest symptoms a person can feel. The fear of a heart attack is real, but most chest pain is not cardiac. It can also come from muscles, the lungs, or anxiety.

This guide covers how to tell muscular, lung, and heart chest pain apart, the red flags that mean you should not wait, and how the ER tells them apart fast.

Why Chest Pain Is Hard to Diagnose at Home

The chest holds the heart, lungs, esophagus, ribs, and many large muscles. All of them can produce sharp or aching pain that radiates and confuses you.

According to MedlinePlus, chest pain has dozens of possible causes ranging from muscle strain to life-threatening events. Self-diagnosis is unreliable because symptoms overlap heavily.

Knowing the patterns helps you decide between waiting it out and calling 911.

Muscular Chest Pain: How It Feels

Muscular chest pain is the most common cause of non-cardiac chest pain. It usually comes from a pulled chest muscle, costochondritis, or rib strain.

Common signs:

  • Sharp pain that worsens with movement. Twisting, reaching, or deep breathing makes it worse.
  • Tenderness when pressed. Pressing on the spot reproduces the pain.
  • Pain stays in one area. It does not spread to the jaw, arm, or back.
  • No other symptoms. No sweating, nausea, or shortness of breath.

For another muscular cause that mimics heart pain, see our slipping rib syndrome guide.

Lung-Related Chest Pain: Pleurisy, Pneumonia, and PE

Pain from the lungs or the lining around them feels different from muscle pain. The breathing connection is the giveaway.

Common signs:

  • Pain that worsens with deep breaths. Each inhale produces a sharp catch.
  • Cough, fever, or colored mucus. Suggests pneumonia or bronchitis.
  • Sudden shortness of breath. Especially after a long flight, surgery, or sitting still for hours.
  • Coughing up blood. Always an ER visit.

MedlinePlus notes that a pulmonary embolism (blood clot in the lung) often presents as sudden chest pain with shortness of breath and can be fatal if untreated. PE is one of the most missed emergencies because the chest pain feels musculoskeletal at first.

Heart-Related Chest Pain: Heart Attack, Angina, Pericarditis

Cardiac chest pain often does not feel “sharp.” It feels like pressure, squeezing, or a heavy weight.

Common signs:

  • Pressure or crushing sensation in the center of the chest.
  • Pain that spreads to the jaw, neck, arm (often left), or back.
  • Other body symptoms. Cold sweats, nausea, lightheadedness, shortness of breath.
  • Pain that lasts more than a few minutes or returns repeatedly.
  • Pain not affected by movement or breathing. Sitting still does not change it.

The CDC reports that women, older adults, and people with diabetes often have atypical heart attack symptoms: jaw pain, fatigue, or nausea without the classic chest pressure.

4 Key Differences That Help You Decide

Question Muscular Lung Heart
Worse with deep breaths? Sometimes Yes, strongly No
Worse with movement? Yes Sometimes No
Tender to press? Yes No No
Sweating, nausea, jaw pain? No Sometimes Often

If your answers point to lung or heart, get evaluated. Muscular pain is the only group where home care is safe to try first.

Red Flags That Need Emergency Care

Call 911 or go to the nearest ER if you have any of these:

  • Pressure or squeezing in the center of the chest lasting more than a few minutes
  • Pain spreading to the jaw, arm, or back
  • Shortness of breath with chest pain
  • Sudden severe chest pain with sweating, nausea, or fainting
  • Coughing up blood
  • Severe pain after long travel or recent surgery (PE risk)

Do not drive yourself if cardiac symptoms are present. An ambulance starts care en route and alerts the ER team.

How ER of Irving Tells Them Apart

At ER of Irving, the chest pain pathway uses imaging and labs to rule the dangerous causes in or out fast:

  • EKG within minutes of arrival to check for cardiac changes
  • Troponin blood test to look for heart muscle damage
  • Chest x-ray for pneumonia, collapsed lung, or fluid
  • CT scan if pulmonary embolism is suspected
  • Physical exam for tenderness, breath sounds, and muscle involvement

Most patients get a clear answer within 60 to 90 minutes.

Call Now Get Direction

FAQs

How long does muscular chest pain last?

Most muscular chest pain improves within 1 to 2 weeks with rest, ice, and over-the-counter pain relief. Persistent pain beyond 3 weeks should be checked.

Can lung problems feel like a heart attack?

Yes. A pulmonary embolism can mimic a heart attack with chest pain and shortness of breath. The ER uses CT imaging and blood tests to tell them apart.

What is costochondritis?

Inflammation of the cartilage that connects ribs to the breastbone. It causes sharp chest pain that worsens with movement and is tender to touch.

Can anxiety cause real chest pain?

Yes. Panic attacks produce chest tightness, racing heart, and shortness of breath that mimic a heart attack. The ER can rule out cardiac causes safely.

Is chest pain on the left side always the heart?

No. The heart sits more centrally than people think. Left-sided chest pain can be muscular, lung, or stomach acid. The ER tests for cardiac causes regardless.

title.rendered: Is it a Stroke? The Critical F.A.S.T. Guide for DFW Residents

content.rendered:
A stroke is one of the most time-sensitive emergencies in medicine. Recognizing it within minutes, not hours, can be the difference between full recovery and lasting brain injury. The F.A.S.T. method makes recognition simple enough for anyone to use.

This guide covers what a stroke is, how to spot one, what to do in the first 5 minutes, and what happens when you arrive at the ER of Irving.

What is a Stroke? Why Every Minute Counts

A stroke happens when blood flow to part of your brain stops. The brain tissue without blood begins dying within minutes, and the damage spreads fast.

Roughly 1.9 million brain cells die every minute during a stroke, according to the American Stroke Association. That is why doctors say “time is brain.” The earlier someone gets to an ER, the more brain tissue can be saved.

Strokes come in two main forms. An ischemic stroke is caused by a clot blocking a brain artery. A hemorrhagic stroke is caused by a brain artery bursting. Both are emergencies, but they need different treatments at the ER.

The F.A.S.T. Method: 4 Warning Signs of Stroke

The CDC and the American Stroke Association both promote F.A.S.T. as the fastest way to recognize a stroke. Each letter points to one thing to check.

  • F – Face drooping. Ask the person to smile. Does one side of the face droop or feel numb?
  • A – Arm weakness. Ask them to raise both arms. Does one arm drift downward or feel heavy?
  • S – Speech difficulty. Ask them to repeat a simple sentence like “the sky is blue.” Are the words slurred or jumbled?
  • T – Time to call 911. Even if symptoms seem to fade, call. Note the exact time symptoms started.

Any one of these signs is enough to call. You do not need all four.

Atypical Stroke Symptoms You Should Not Miss

F.A.S.T. catches most strokes, but not all. The American Stroke Association warns about signs that are easy to dismiss.

Women often have a sudden severe headache, nausea, hiccups, or a feeling that something is wrong without a clear face or arm symptom. Younger adults can have strokes too. Vision loss in one eye, sudden severe dizziness, or trouble walking should not be brushed off.

Posterior strokes affect the back of the brain. They often cause balance and vision problems instead of the classic face droop. Silent strokes show up on a CT scan with no obvious symptoms at the time.

If something is sudden and severe, call 911. Even atypical strokes need the same urgent ER pathway.

Ischemic vs Hemorrhagic Stroke: Why the Difference Matters

The two types of stroke need opposite treatments. That is why the ER team moves fast to identify which one is happening.

About 87% of strokes are ischemic, per MedlinePlus. A blood clot blocks an artery in the brain. If the patient arrives within 3 to 4.5 hours of symptom onset, doctors can use a clot-dissolving drug called tPA to restore blood flow. After that window, the drug can do more harm than good.

The remaining strokes are hemorrhagic. A brain blood vessel ruptures and bleeds. tPA would make this worse. These patients need blood pressure control, sometimes surgery, and intensive care.

A CT scan within the first hour at the ER is what tells the team which type they are dealing with.

The First 5 Minutes: Exactly What To Do

What you do in the first 5 minutes matters more than almost anything else.

  1. Call 911 immediately. Do not call a friend or search online. Just dial.
  2. Note the exact time symptoms started. Or the last time the person was definitely normal. This number decides whether tPA is on the table.
  3. Stay with them. Help them sit or lie down safely. Loosen tight clothing.
  4. Track any changes. Symptoms can worsen quickly. Tell the paramedics what changed.
  5. Do not give food, water, or medicine. Swallowing may be impaired. Anything by mouth can choke them.

Ambulances also notify the ER en route, so the stroke team is ready when you arrive.

What Not To Do: 4 Mistakes That Cost Critical Minutes

These four mistakes happen often and waste the only thing that matters: time.

  • Don’t drive them yourself. An ambulance alerts the ER in advance and starts care en route. A private car arrives cold.
  • Don’t give aspirin. Aspirin makes hemorrhagic strokes worse. The ER decides after the CT scan.
  • Don’t wait to see if it passes. Symptoms that fade can be a TIA, or mini-stroke. About 1 in 3 TIA patients have a full stroke within a year.
  • Don’t let them sleep it off. Stroke symptoms during sleep are how the time window gets missed. If you can’t say when symptoms started, tPA usually isn’t possible.

Stroke Risk Factors and Prevention for DFW Adults

Most strokes are preventable. The CDC lists the major risk factors, and most are within your control.

High blood pressure is the single biggest risk factor. Controlling it cuts stroke risk roughly in half. Diabetes, high cholesterol, atrial fibrillation, smoking, and obesity each raise the odds on their own.

Texas-specific concerns add up too:

  • Summer heat. Dehydration thickens blood and can trigger ischemic strokes in vulnerable adults. Drink water on hot days.
  • Sleep apnea. Common and underdiagnosed in DFW. Untreated sleep apnea doubles stroke risk.
  • Age over 55. Risk doubles every decade after.

What helps: regular blood pressure checks, taking prescribed medications consistently, 30 minutes of moderate exercise most days, and not smoking. Atrial fibrillation needs aggressive management because it raises stroke risk fivefold.

What Happens When You Arrive at the ER of Irving for a Suspected Stroke

At the ER of Irving, the stroke pathway starts the moment paramedics call ahead. Per NINDS stroke care guidelines, the goal is to compress every minute that matters:

  • First 15 minutes. Vital signs, blood draw, neurological exam by an ER physician.
  • Within 25 minutes. CT scan of the head to rule in or rule out bleeding.
  • Within 45 minutes. CT results read, neurologist consulted.
  • Within 60 minutes. Decision on tPA for ischemic strokes, or transfer to a comprehensive stroke center if needed.

Our 24/7 ER team is set up to keep the tPA window open. We coordinate with regional comprehensive stroke centers for cases that need endovascular thrombectomy or neurosurgery.

If you suspect a stroke, call 911 and tell them to bring the patient here.

Call Now Get Direction

FAQs

How long after symptoms start is tPA still effective?

Up to 4.5 hours from symptom onset for most patients. Some select cases extend further. After that window, the risk of brain bleeding from tPA outweighs the benefit. Mechanical thrombectomy can extend the treatment window to 24 hours in some patients.

Can young people have strokes?

Yes. About 10 to 15% of strokes happen in adults under 50. Causes include heart conditions, blood clotting disorders, drug use, and head trauma. Sudden severe headache or vision loss in a young adult should not be dismissed.

What does a mini-stroke feel like?

A transient ischemic attack, or TIA, produces stroke-like symptoms that resolve within 24 hours, usually within an hour. The brain isn’t permanently damaged, but a TIA is a strong warning sign. About 1 in 3 TIA patients have a full stroke within a year. Get evaluated.

Can stress trigger a stroke?

Chronic stress raises blood pressure and inflammation, both of which raise stroke risk. Acute emotional stress can trigger strokes in already-vulnerable adults, but it is rarely the sole cause.

What is the difference between a heart attack and a stroke?

A heart attack is a blockage in a heart artery, usually causing chest pain. A stroke is a blockage or bleed in a brain artery, causing neurological symptoms like face droop or speech trouble. Both need 911.

What is the recovery time after a stroke?

It varies. Many patients see meaningful recovery in 3 to 6 months with rehabilitation. Some have permanent deficits. The faster the initial treatment, the better the outcomes.

title.rendered: Heat Stroke vs. Heat Exhaustion: Knowing the Difference in Irving, TX

content.rendered:
Heat exhaustion and heat stroke are stages of the same emergency, and the difference shows in the mind. Heavy sweating with weakness, dizziness, and clammy skin points to heat exhaustion. Confusion, a core temperature of 103°F or higher, or passing out means heat stroke, and that is a 911 call. Both usually begin with fluid loss, which is why early dehydration treatment matters. This guide shows you how to tell the two apart and what to do in the first ten minutes.

Why Heat Safety Matters in Irving

North Texas heat is a humidity problem as much as a temperature problem. According to the CDC, sweat evaporates slowly in humid air, so your body loses its main way of cooling itself. Once that system falls behind, “overheated” can turn into a medical crisis quickly.

Irving’s average August highs reach 95°F or more, per WeatherSpark climate data. Long afternoons at that level are exactly when heat illness shows up at local parks, job sites, and festivals.

What is Heat Exhaustion? Recognizing the Early Warning Signs

Heat exhaustion is your body signaling it has reached its limit. The CDC describes it as the result of losing too much water and salt through heavy sweating. It is serious, but with fast action it usually does not require a hospital stay.

The CDC lists these warning signs:

  • Heavy, profuse sweating
  • Cold, pale, and clammy skin
  • A fast but weak pulse
  • Nausea, vomiting, or muscle cramps
  • Feeling faint, dizzy, or unusually tired
  • A mild headache

What is Heat Stroke? A Life-Threatening Emergency

Heat stroke means the body’s temperature regulation has failed. Core temperature can climb to 103°F or higher within minutes, and the CDC warns that untreated heat stroke can cause permanent disability or death. The hallmark is a change in mental status.

  • High body temperature: 103°F or higher
  • Altered mental state: confusion, slurred speech, agitation, or loss of consciousness
  • Skin changes: hot and red, either dry or damp; sweating may stop entirely
  • Pulse: fast, strong, and pounding
  • Neurological signs: seizures or fainting

It also arrives two different ways. Classic heat stroke builds over days of heat exposure and tends to strike older adults indoors. Exertional heat stroke hits athletes and outdoor workers mid-effort, often while they are still sweating heavily.

At ER of Irving, heat stroke emergency treatment means rapid cooling, IV fluids, and continuous monitoring to bring core temperature down fast.

Heat Exhaustion vs Heat Stroke: Symptom Comparison Chart

Feature Heat Exhaustion Heat Stroke
Core temperature Often below 103°F 103°F or higher
Skin Cold, pale, clammy, sweaty Hot and red, dry or damp
Pulse Fast and weak Fast and strong
Mental state Faint or dizzy, but alert Confused, slurring, or unconscious
Sweating Heavy sweating May have stopped
What to do Cool place, sip water Call 911, cool fast, no drinks

What To Do Right Now: First Aid by Severity

The first ten minutes decide how a heat emergency ends. Match your response to what you see.

If it looks like heat exhaustion

  1. Move to a cool place. Shade helps; an air-conditioned building is better.
  2. Cool the skin. Apply cool, wet cloths or take a cool bath.
  3. Loosen clothing. Remove heavy or restrictive layers.
  4. Sip water slowly. The CDC advises small sips only while the person is alert and not vomiting.

Escalate to emergency care if vomiting starts, symptoms last longer than one hour, or the person keeps getting worse despite cooling, per CDC guidance.

If it looks like heat stroke

  • Call 911 immediately. Do not drive the person yourself if they are confused or fading.
  • Get them out of the sun and into the coolest spot available.
  • Cool aggressively. The CDC recommends cool water immersion, a garden hose, or ice packs on the neck, armpits, and groin.
  • Do not give anything to drink. A confused person may not swallow safely, and choking is a real risk.

Who is Most at Risk in the Texas Heat?

Anyone can overheat, but the CDC flags several groups that need extra caution:

  • Infants and young children, whose bodies regulate temperature less efficiently
  • Adults 65 and older, especially those taking medications that change how the body handles heat
  • People with chronic illness, including heart disease, high blood pressure, and obesity
  • Outdoor workers and athletes who spend hours in direct sun

Never leave a child, an older adult, or a pet in a parked car. Cabin temperatures in a Texas summer climb to dangerous levels within minutes, even with windows cracked. For a full prevention playbook covering hydration schedules, clothing, and timing, see our Texas summer heat safety guide.

Don’t Guess With Heat Illness. Get Emergency Care Fast

If someone is confused, fainting, vomiting, or not improving after 30 minutes of cooling, treat it as an emergency. Heat illness and dehydration travel together, and our team treats both around the clock, from IV fluids for dehydration to full heat stroke care.

Walk in any hour at 8200 N MacArthur Blvd, Suite 110, Irving, TX, or call (972) 893-3148. For life-threatening symptoms, call 911 first.

FAQs

Can heat exhaustion turn into heat stroke?

Yes, and it can happen fast. When cooling and rehydration do not start promptly, core temperature keeps climbing until the body’s regulation system fails. Treat heat exhaustion as a warning: get cool, sip water, and watch the person’s mental state closely over the next hour.

What temperature is considered heat stroke?

A core body temperature of 103°F or higher, together with any change in mental state, signals heat stroke under CDC criteria. Home thermometers can read lower than true core temperature, so never wait on a number when someone is confused, slurring words, or losing consciousness.

Why shouldn’t I give a heat stroke victim water?

Heat stroke alters the mind. A confused or semi-conscious person may not be able to swallow safely, so drinking risks choking or fluid entering the lungs. Focus on rapid external cooling with water on the skin and ice packs, and let emergency providers handle fluids by IV.

How long does it take to recover from heat exhaustion?

Most people improve within a few hours once they cool down and rehydrate, though resting for the remainder of the day is wise. Symptoms that last beyond one hour, or vomiting that keeps fluids from staying down, mean you should be evaluated by a doctor.

Should I go to the ER for heat exhaustion?

Go if symptoms persist past an hour, vomiting will not stop, or fluids will not stay down. Confusion, fainting, or hot dry skin skips the wait-and-see stage entirely: call 911. When in doubt, an exam with labs and IV fluids settles the question quickly.

title.rendered: Emergency Room of Irving, TX vs. Urgent Care: What’s the Difference?

content.rendered:
Quick answer: If your symptoms could be life threatening, go to the emergency room or call 911. Chest pain, stroke signs, trouble breathing, and heavy bleeding all need emergency care.

Urgent care handles minor illness and injury, but only while it is open. ER of Irving is open 24 hours a day, every day of the year.

This guide explains which conditions belong in each setting, what changes after hours, and how to decide when you are not sure.

When should you go to the emergency room?

Go to the ER for any symptom that could threaten your life, your limb, or your sight. MedlinePlus advises calling 911 when you think a problem is life threatening, even if you are not certain.

Take these symptoms to an emergency room right away:

  • Chest pain or pressure, especially with sweating, nausea, or arm and jaw pain
  • Stroke signs such as face drooping, arm weakness, or slurred speech
  • Trouble breathing or severe shortness of breath
  • Bleeding that will not stop with steady pressure
  • Head injury with confusion, vomiting, or loss of consciousness
  • Seizures, fainting, or a sudden severe headache
  • Severe abdominal pain
  • Suspected poisoning or overdose
  • High fever in a newborn, or a child who will not wake fully

Chest discomfort is the most common heart attack sign, and it usually lasts more than a few minutes. It can feel like pressure, squeezing, or fullness rather than sharp pain, according to MedlinePlus. Women more often report nausea, cold sweats, or unusual fatigue.

When is urgent care the right choice?

Urgent care suits minor problems that still need same day attention. Common examples include mild flu symptoms, small cuts, earaches, and simple urinary infections.

Two things decide it for you. The first is how severe the symptom is. The second is whether urgent care is actually open.

What if it is late at night or on a weekend?

Most urgent care centers around Irving close in the evening and keep shorter weekend hours. An emergency room does not close.

That matters because symptoms rarely wait for business hours. ER of Irving is staffed around the clock by emergency physicians, with lab and imaging on site. If you need care at 2 in the morning in Irving, an emergency room is the option that is open.

ER or urgent care in Irving: a side by side look

Feature Emergency room Urgent care
Best for Life, limb, or sight threatening symptoms Minor illness and injury
Hours Open 24 hours, every day Extended hours, not overnight
Staffing Emergency physicians on site at all times Varies by location and shift
On site testing Advanced imaging and full lab Basic X-ray and lab
Appointment Never needed Walk in or booked
Typical cost Higher, varies by plan Lower, varies by plan

What is a freestanding emergency room?

A freestanding emergency room is a licensed emergency facility that does not sit on a hospital campus. It is open 24 hours, staffed by emergency physicians, and equipped for advanced imaging and lab work.

Freestanding ERs treat the same range of emergencies as any emergency department. When a patient needs surgery, intensive care, or admission, the ER stabilizes them and arranges transfer to a partner hospital.

What does an emergency visit cost in Irving?

Cost depends on your insurance plan, your deductible, and the care you receive. An emergency visit generally costs more than an urgent care visit. Emergency facilities keep physicians, imaging, and lab staff available at every hour of the day.

Check your coverage before you need it. Our insurance and billing page lists the plans we work with and explains how to ask about your out of pocket cost.

Never delay care for a life threatening symptom because of cost. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between urgent care and an emergency room?

Urgent care treats minor illness and injury during set hours. An emergency room treats conditions that could threaten life, limb, or sight, and it stays open 24 hours. Emergency rooms also keep advanced imaging, full lab services, and emergency physicians on site at all times.

Can an emergency room treat minor problems too?

Yes. ER of Irving treats fractures, sore throat, rashes, and similar concerns alongside true emergencies. This matters most when urgent care is closed.

Where should I take my child?

Children with a high fever, breathing trouble, dehydration, or a significant injury should be seen in an emergency room. Our pediatric emergency team treats children of all ages, 24 hours a day.

Do I need an appointment?

No. Emergency rooms accept walk in patients at any hour, and no referral is required.

When should I call 911 instead of driving?

Call 911 for chest pain, stroke signs, severe breathing trouble, major trauma, or anyone who is unresponsive. Paramedics begin treatment on the way. MedlinePlus advises calling if you think a problem is life threatening, even when you are unsure.

Call Now Get Directions

If you think you are having a medical emergency, call 911 or go to your nearest emergency room immediately.
